title: The four hinges (CCC 1805–1809)
hook: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, on which a good life turns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the theological virtues: faith, hope and charity, given by God. Your line was the greatest is charity. Today, four more virtues, the ones people build by practice.

Look at the nearest door. It's heavy, maybe solid wood, maybe steel. But everything it does, opening, closing, letting people in, keeping the cold out, depends on a few small pieces of metal on one side that you never look at. The hinges. Take them off and the best door in the world is just a slab leaning against a wall. The ancient world had a word for hinge, and the Church borrowed it to name four virtues. The same word turns up on men in red hats.
screen: `A HEAVY DOOR.` → `SMALL PIECES OF METAL.` → `WITHOUT THEM, A SLAB.`

segments.voice: Cardinal comes from the Latin cardo: hinge. The cardinal virtues are the four on which a good life turns, and the cardinals of the Church carry the same word. The four are old. Greek philosophers like Plato named them long before Christ. The book of Wisdom names them too, in the Douay-Rheims: "she teacheth temperance, and prudence, and justice, and fortitude." Christian writers like Ambrose and Augustine took them up, and the Church still teaches them. Prudence is practical wisdom: seeing what's actually good here, now, and the right way to do it. The Catechism calls it the charioteer of the virtues, because it steers the others. Justice is the steady will to give God and neighbor what is their due. Fortitude is courage and firmness: holding on to the good when it's hard, resisting fear, even the fear of death. Temperance is balance: enjoying good things without being ruled by them. Here's the difference from yesterday. Faith, hope and charity, Catholics say, are given. These four are human virtues, built by practice, choice by choice, like muscles, and God's grace helps them grow. Keep telling the truth when it's awkward, and you become just. Keep saying enough, and you become temperate. The door swings easier every time.
screen: `CARDO: HINGE.` · `PLATO, WISDOM, AMBROSE.` · `PRUDENCE STEERS THE OTHERS.` · `BUILT BY PRACTICE, LIKE MUSCLE.` · then, large: `TEMPERANCE, PRUDENCE, JUSTICE, FORTITUDE.`

segments.voice: Say the four slowly: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. Then ask which door in your life is sticking: prudence for a decision, justice for someone you owe something to, even just credit, fortitude for a hard conversation, or temperance for the thing you tend to overdo. Choose one and picture using it in one specific moment; if you pray, you can ask for help with it.
Cardinal virtues. From the Latin for hinge: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance, the four human virtues on which a good life turns. Today's word.
Your line: the hinges. Small pieces of metal, and a whole door swings on them. Day three hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching, from catechism classes to confession, uses the four cardinal virtues as a map of the good life, and some Catholics choose one to work on during a season like Lent.
